title: Spot the unsupported policy claims
scenario: You pasted your refund policy into a chat and asked whether change-of-mind returns are allowed. The AI answered — compare every sentence of the answer against the policy excerpt you supplied.
task: Select every part of the AI answer that is NOT supported by the pasted policy text.
response:
POLICY (excerpt you pasted): “Refunds are available within 30 days of purchase for unused items in original packaging. Shipping costs are non-refundable. Change-of-mind returns follow the same 30-day window.”

AI ANSWER: Yes — you can return unused items within 30 days in original packaging. Change-of-mind returns follow the same window. Shipping costs are non-refundable, unless the item arrived damaged, in which case shipping is refunded. Refunds are processed within 5 business days.

claims.text: “you can return unused items within 30 days in original packaging”
claims.feedback: Supported — this paraphrases the policy's first sentence almost word for word.
Supported — the excerpt states exactly this.

claims.text: “unless the item arrived damaged, in which case shipping is refunded”
claims.feedback: NOT in the excerpt. A plausible-sounding exception invented beyond the source — precisely the kind of addition grounding is designed to catch.
No such timeline appears in the policy text. Gap-filling specifics read exactly like policy language — and are the most dangerous kind of addition.
Supported — a direct paraphrase of the second sentence.

hints: Compare each sentence to the excerpt: does its meaning appear there?
Specifics absent from the source — exceptions, timelines, numbers — are the suspects.
explanation: Grounded answers can be checked line by line: supported claims trace back to the source, invented extras read just as fluently as the real ones. The skill is comparing each statement to the pasted text — not trusting the tone of the answer.
